Supplement_PREBAL.csv.description: Verbatim author PREBAL rationale and adjustments, online supplement section 4
rows: Alien species included in this study. Information regarding date of first record is based on Galil (2007), Golani (2010) and other sources (http://www.ciesm.org/online/atlas/). The numbers in the last column of the table identify the functional groups of the Israeli Mediterranean continental shelf model (Table 1 of the manuscript or Supplement Online Information section 1).

Outputs of the models to consider that the model is balanced. R/A = respiration/assimilation ratio; R/B = respiration/biomass ratio (year-1); and NE = net efficiency. In addition, EE and P/Q were checked (Table 1 of the manuscript). Dem. = demersal

The pre-balancing analysis (PREBAL) was designed to assess the data quality before the mass balance process and/or dynamic simulations are developed with Ecopath and Ecosim food web models in order to ensure that the input data are reasonable and robust and to indirectly verify model accuracy and robustness (Link, 2010). Therefore, once the input data has been collected and analysed, it is needed to test the model through the PREBAL analysis (Heymans et al., 2016).

Link (2010) describes a set of diagnostics that can be tested thought graphical representation, including biomass and vital rates vital rates across taxa and trophic levels, biomass and vital rates ratios, and total production and removals.

In this study, we checked the diagnostics related to biomass and vital rates (P/B and Q/B) across taxa and trophic levels. Biomass and vital rates of each functional group were plotted along the x-axis in order of decreasing trophic level. In the biomass diagnostic, we check the two rules that Link (2010) proposed: 1) the range of biomass should span 5-7 orders of magnitude and 2) the slope should decline by 5-10% with increasing trophic level across all the taxa. In addition, biomass and vital rates of predators should be lower than prey. For all of these diagnostics, groups with values that greatly exceed or fall below the general trend were examined.

Results of the PREBAL analysis in both time periods are shown in Fig. 1 (1990s) and Fig. 2 (2010s). Both models complied with the two rules that we checked for biomass as the range of biomass spanned 5 orders of magnitude and the slope declined by 5.5% and 6.1% in 1990s and 2010s time periods, respectively.

The overall diagnostics applied to our models showed general coherent reduction of parameters values with increasing trophic levels (Fig. 1 and 2). Regarding biomass, in 2010s period all the functional groups were represented, while in the 1990s period, new alien demersal fishes (functional group or F.G. 24) and alien medium pelagic fishes (F.G. 35) were not present because they did not invaded the ecosystem yet (Fig. 1). In both models, sea birds (F.G. 38) presented low biomass despite their trophic position (Fig. 1a and 2a).  This is due to their uncertainty of biomass estimates and their trophic positions in Ecopath models, as an important part of their diet are discards, which EwE considers as a detritus group with TL = 1.

The results also showed that phytoplankton (F.G.1), micro and mesozooplankton (F.G. 3), polychaetes (F.G. 6), benthic invertebrates (F.G. 12), small pelagic fishes (F.G. 31), small native demersal fishes (F.G. 20), native medium pelagic fishes (F.G. 34) and large pelagic fishes (F.G. 36) could potentially be overestimated, while benthic primary producers (F.G. 2), alien herbivorous (F.G. 22), demersal fishes in the upper slope (F.G. 26) and dolphins could be underestimated in both time periods (Fig. 1a and 2a). As expected by Link (2010), groups at the two extremes (in the ICS models, phytoplankton (F.G. 1) and dolphins (F.G. 39)) tend to present out of trend biomass values. In the case of small native demersal fishes (F.G. 20), we can justify their higher biomass due to the large number of species included in this group. For native medium pelagic fishes (F.G. 34) and large pelagic fishes (F.G. 36), the last one with biomass estimate based on stock assessment, we could expect lower biomass but the requirements of the model imposed higher biomass mainly due to their large catch, as their predation mortalities showed low values (Table 2 in the manuscript). For the remainder groups, biomass estimates were calculated by the model, showing the need of stock assessment for these groups. In absence of biomass estimates, adjustments on the diet matrix were needed in order to ensure the correct diagnostic in PREBAL.

Moreover, in the 1990s period, large native demersal fishes (F.G. 21) presented a high biomass. We could assume that their biomass estimate was overestimated but, as in other cases, the large catch imposed high requirements to the model, as their predation mortalities showed low values (Table 1 in the manuscript). This group did not show a high biomass in the 2010s period due to its overexploitation during the period.

Benthic primary producers (F.G. 2) and alien herbivorous (F.G. 22) presented low biomass values as these groups live exclusively in the shallow waters, while the model included depths from 0 to 200 m. Therefore, we could expect low biomasses for these groups. Demersal fishes in the upper slope (F.G. 26) also showed low biomass estimates. These could be related to the lower number of hauls in these strata on the trawl survey used to estimate biomasses and/or to the deep-sea faunal and biomass impoverishment of the Eastern Mediterranean Sea compared to the western basin (Goren and Galil, 2002).

In addition, alien crabs (F.G. 11) and native crabs (F.G. 10) showed low biomass in 1990s and 2010s time periods, respectively (Fig. 1a and 2a). We could expect these results as the biomass of alien crabs (F.G. 11) increased during the periods while the biomass of native crabs decreased although the native crabs (F.G. 10) did not present high values in 1990s period.

Finally, mullets (F.G. 15) and hake (F.G. 17) showed low biomass estimates in the 2010s period as a result of overexploitation and niche displacement to deeper water by their alien competitors (goatfishes (F.G. 16) and alien lizardfish (F.G. 25)) (Galil and Zenetos, 2002; Rilov and Galil, 2009).

In the ICS model, P/B ratios for alien herbivorous (F.G. 22), benthic invertebrates (F.G. 12), turtles (F.G. 37) and dolphins (F.G. 39) were low, while those for phytoplankton (F.G. 1), micro and mesozooplankton (F.G. 3), macrozooplankton (F.G. 4), gelatinous plankton (F.G. 5) and benthopelagic cephalopods (F.G. 14) were high (Fig. 1b and 2b). Initial P/B values for macrozooplankton (F.G. 4), polychaetes (F.G. 6) and suprabenthos (F.G. 7) were modified as we were able to find better parameters estimates taking into account the PREBAL analysis. For macrozooplankton (F.G. 4), initial P/B value was 22.92 (from Labat and Cuzin-Roudy (1996)), and as this value was high we decided to apply a P/Q of 0.3 taking into account the P/Q of 0.33 for micro and mesozooplankton (F.G. 3). For polychaetes (F.G. 6) and suprabenthos (F.G. 7), initial P/B values were weighted values of different species but they were low. Therefore, we decided to use the maximum value. For the other problematic groups, in absence of better parameter estimates, we decided to use common values in other Ecopath models set up in the Mediterranean Sea (Coll et al., 2006; Coll et al., 2007; Tsagarakis et al., 2010; Corrales et al., 2015).

Finally, in the ICS model, Q/B ratios for alien herbivorous (F.G. 22), benthic invertebrates (F.G. 12), shrimps (F.G. 8 and 9), crabs (F.G. 10 and 11), rocky fishes (F.G. 19) and turtles (F.G. 37) were low, while those for micro and mesozooplankton (F.G. 3), macrozooplankton (F.G. 4), gelatinous plankton (F.G. 5), suprabenthos (F.G. 7), benthopelagic cephalopods (F.G. 14), sea birds (F.G. 38) and dolphins were high. Q/B ratios for shrimps (F.G. 8 and 9), crabs (F.G. 10 and 11), rocky fishes (F.G. 19), seabirds (F.G. 38) and dolphins (F.G. 39) were maintained as they came from empirical equations (See Supplement Online Information section 1). Initial Q/B ratios for alien herbivorous (F.G. 22) and demersal sharks (F.G. 29) were modified as those had low and high P/Q ratios respectively. For alien herbivorous (F.G. 22) we decided to apply a high P/Q ratio (0.25) and for demersal sharks (F.G. 29) a low P/Q (0.15), taking into account their trophic position and ecological principles. The other problematic groups, in absence of better parameter estimates and as for P/B ratios, we decided to use common values in other Ecopath models set up in the Mediterranean Sea (Coll et al., 2006; Coll et al., 2007; Tsagarakis et al., 2010; Corrales et al., 2015).

To conclude, the PREBAL analysis applied to the ICS model showed that in general the models complied general ecological principles. Moreover, it showed that for some groups, better information is required, mainly for planktonic groups, which should inform future scientific research objectives in the area. As new information is being generated, the models could be updated and therefore, its quality and reliability increased. In addition, with the calibration of the 1990s model to available historical data, some of these parameters should be rechecked and therefore data input of the model may improve.
